passages.happening:
The people make Josiah's son Jehoahaz king, and after three months the king of Egypt removes him, lays a levy on Judah, makes his brother Eliakim king, renames him Jehoiakim, and carries Jehoahaz off to Egypt (verses 1-4). Jehoiakim reigns eleven years and does evil; ‘Then Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jehoiakim and bound him with bronze shackles to take him to Babylon’ (verse 6), and takes some of the temple's vessels for his own temple (verse 7).

Jehoiachin reigns three months and ten days and is taken to Babylon with the temple's treasures (verses 9-10). Zedekiah reigns eleven years, ‘And he did evil in the sight of the LORD his God and did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke for the LORD’ (verse 12). He rebels against Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God, ‘But Zedekiah stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
This is the end of the story Chronicles has told since Adam: the line of David, the temple, and the people gathered around it. The four kings are covered in brief, formula paragraphs, each briefer than any earlier reign, as though the story were running out of breath.

Jehoahaz reigned three months in 609 BC before Neco removed him. Jehoiakim, Egypt's appointee, ruled about 609 to 598 BC and became Babylon's vassal after Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC. Jehoiachin reigned three months before surrendering; the Babylonian Chronicle, a cuneiform record of the empire's years, dates Jerusalem's capture to early 597 BC, and Babylonian tablets later list food rations for Jehoiachin, king of Judah, in Babylon. Zedekiah, put on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar, rebelled. Conquerors renamed vassal kings as a sign of their authority and carried temple treasures to their own gods' temples as trophies.

Verse 6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim to take him to Babylon, while 2 Kings 24 says only that he rested with his fathers and was succeeded by his son, which suggests he died as king in Judah; whether he was actually taken away is uncertain. Who to notice: Zedekiah, the last king, who would not humble himself. The word of 7:14 has its last test here, and it is refused.
passages.later: Second Kings says of Jehoiakim, ‘And Jehoiakim rested with his fathers, and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place’ (2 Kings 24:6).
passages.asks: Zedekiah stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning. Ask where you are holding out against God out of pride. And ask what it would cost to humble yourself before the word you already know.

passages.t: Again and again, until there was no remedy
passages.happening:
The leaders of the priests and the people multiply their unfaithfulness and defile the house of the LORD (verse 14). ‘Again and again the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent word to His people through His messengers because He had compassion on them and on His dwelling place’ (verse 15). ‘But they mocked the messengers of God, despising His words and scoffing at His prophets, until the wrath of the LORD against His people was stirred up beyond remedy’ (verse 16).

The king of the Chaldeans comes, and many are killed (verse 17). Nebuchadnezzar carries off the temple's vessels and treasures to Babylon (verse 18). ‘Then the Chaldeans set fire to the house of God and broke down the wall of Jerusalem’ (verse 19). Those who escape are carried into exile in Babylon and serve him and his sons until Persia comes to power (verse 20). ‘So the land enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation, until seventy years were completed, in fulfillment of the word of the LORD through Jeremiah’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Jerusalem fell after a long siege in 587 or 586 BC, and the temple was burned. The fuller accounts are in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52. The Chronicler does not linger on the siege; he tells it in a few plain lines and gives the reason he has taught in every reign. These notes do not linger either.

Verses 15 and 16 are among the most important in the book. God sent his messengers again and again because he had compassion, chamal; the same word returns in verse 17 in the negative, as the Babylonians show no pity. The people mocked until the wrath rose beyond remedy, marpe, healing, the word that recalls the promise to heal the land of a humble people. Judgment came after long mercy and many warnings.

The land's Sabbaths draw on the law's command that the land rest every seventh year, and its warning that if Israel refused, the land would enjoy its Sabbaths while the people were in exile. The seventy years come from Jeremiah. The Chronicler joins Leviticus and Jeremiah to read the exile as judgment and as a kind of forced rest, a desolation that also prepared for renewal.
passages.later: The law had warned, ‘Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate, while you are in the land of your enemies’ (Leviticus 26:34). Jeremiah had said, ‘these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years’ (Jeremiah 25:11).
passages.hard:
If God chose Jerusalem and promised David a lasting house, how could he let the city and the temple burn? And what does this chapter say about suffering, then and now?

This was the question that faced the exiles, and much of the Old Testament wrestles with it. Lamentations grieves the city's fall without pretending to understand everything, and Psalm 89 cries out that God seems to have renounced his covenant with David. Both are in the Bible.

Chronicles gives its own answer, and it is not the answer of a God who was quick to anger. God sent word again and again because he had compassion on his people and on his house. The promise to David had always carried conditions for each king, and Solomon had heard the warning that the house could become a heap of rubble. The city fell because king and people refused the messengers for generations. The destruction does not show that God was unfaithful; it shows that he meant what he said. And the book does not end here.

This is Judah's own Scripture, judging Judah's own kings and grieving Judah's own losses. It was written for people who had lost everything, to help them understand their history and turn back to God. It is not a key for reading anyone else's suffering. It gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved: not a city under siege, not a people driven from its home, not a family that has lost everything. And it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: God sent word again and again because he had compassion. Ask what messengers God has sent you, and how you have treated them. And ask whether you believe that his warnings come from compassion.

passages.happening: ‘In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation throughout his kingdom and to put it in writing’ (verse 22). Cyrus declares that the LORD, the God of heaven, has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and appointed him to build a house for him at Jerusalem: ‘Whoever among you belongs to His people, may the LORD his God be with him, and may he go up’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The book does not end in ruins. Its final words are a door opening: a foreign king, moved by the LORD, invites the exiles to go up and rebuild. Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BC, and in his first year as its ruler, 539 or 538 BC, he issued this decree, which is repeated at the start of Ezra. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay inscription in the British Museum, records his policy of returning displaced peoples and their gods to their homelands, though it does not mention Judah. Calling the LORD the God of heaven fits the respectful language Persian rulers used toward their subjects' gods. To stir, ur, is the language Chronicles uses when God moves foreign kings.

Verses 21 and 22 mirror each other: Jeremiah's word is fulfilled in the desolation and again in the decree. In the traditional Hebrew order Chronicles is the last book, so the Hebrew Scriptures close on this invitation. The book's last word in Hebrew means and let him go up, an ending that points forward rather than closing the story.

The line of David survived the exile. Matthew's genealogy treats the deportation to Babylon as one of the great turning points of Israel's history, alongside Abraham and David, and names Jehoiachin, Jechoniah, in the line that leads to Jesus.
passages.later: Ezra opens with the same decree: ‘In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah’ (Ezra 1:1). Matthew counts ‘fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ’ (Matthew 1:17).
passages.hard:
How do the seventy years of exile add up?

Jeremiah prophesied seventy years for Babylon's rule, and the Chronicler applies the number to the land's desolation. Interpreters count it in different ways. Some measure from Nebuchadnezzar's first move against Jerusalem around 605 BC to Cyrus's decree in 539 or 538 BC, roughly seventy years. Others count from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC to its rebuilding, finished around 516 BC, also about seventy years. Others take seventy as a round number meaning a full lifetime, the complete span of a judgment. Each takes the prophecy seriously; they differ over whether it was meant as an exact count or a symbolic whole.
passages.asks: The last word of the book is an invitation: may he go up. Ask what God is inviting you to go up and rebuild. And ask what ruin in your life you have treated as the end of the story.
